title: Hydrocodone and Alcohol: Why Mixing Is Dangerous (Norco, Vicodin)
excerpt: Why hydrocodone and alcohol are a dangerous mix: how both slow your breathing, the FDA boxed warning, the extra liver risk with Norco and Vicodin, how long to wait, and what to do in an overdose.
metaDescription: Can you drink on hydrocodone, Norco, or Vicodin? How alcohol and opioids slow breathing, the FDA boxed warning, how long to wait, and overdose signs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** don't drink alcohol while you're taking hydrocodone. This is one of the drug-and-alcohol combinations where even a small amount can be genuinely dangerous. Hydrocodone (sold as Norco, Vicodin, Lortab, Hysingla ER, Zohydro ER, and in some prescription cough syrups) and alcohol both slow down the part of your brain that keeps you breathing. Together they can slow it far more than either one alone, and the main way people die from this mix is that their breathing becomes too slow or shallow while they're asleep. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) puts this risk in a boxed warning, its strongest kind, on opioid products like hydrocodone.

**The quick rules:** Avoid alcohol completely for as long as you're taking hydrocodone, including the evening after your last dose. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist how long to wait after your final dose before drinking, because the answer depends on the product and on you. Most hydrocodone pills also contain acetaminophen (the drug in Tylenol), which adds a liver risk on top of the breathing risk. Keep naloxone (Narcan) in the house if anyone there takes opioids. And if someone who has mixed the two is very hard to wake, breathing slowly, snoring or gurgling in an unusual way, or has blue or gray lips, call 911 right away.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and the official label warnings. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and the exact product you take. **Talk to your prescriber or pharmacist before drinking any alcohol if you take hydrocodone in any form**, including Norco, Vicodin, Lortab, Hysingla ER, Zohydro ER, hydrocodone with ibuprofen, or a hydrocodone cough medicine. Any decision about alcohol while you're on this medicine should come from your prescriber, not from an article. **Call 911 immediately if** someone who has taken hydrocodone and alcohol can't be woken up, is breathing very slowly or irregularly, has pinpoint pupils, has blue or gray lips or fingertips, or is making choking or gurgling sounds. If you have naloxone, give it and still call 911. In the US, Poison Control is at **1-800-222-1222** for questions that aren't emergencies.

## How Hydrocodone and Alcohol Interact: The Real Mechanism

Hydrocodone is an opioid pain reliever, closely related to oxycodone and codeine. It works by attaching to **mu-opioid receptors**, docking sites found throughout your brain, spinal cord, and gut. That's how it blocks pain. But some of those receptors sit in the **brainstem**, the part of your brain that runs your breathing automatically, without you thinking about it.

Your brainstem constantly checks the level of carbon dioxide in your blood. When carbon dioxide rises, it tells you to breathe faster and deeper. Opioids dull that reflex. Your brain stops responding as strongly to rising carbon dioxide, so breathing gets slower and shallower. Doctors call this **respiratory depression**, and it's the main reason opioid overdoses are fatal.

Alcohol works through different pathways. It boosts **GABA**, the brain's main "slow down" signal, and blocks some of the brain's "speed up" signals. The result is a general dampening of the nervous system: sleepiness, slower reactions, poorer coordination, and at higher amounts, slower breathing as well.

Put the two together and the effects stack. Two substances that each push breathing down, by different routes, can push it down much further as a pair. Alcohol also makes you sleepier, and sleep is exactly when this matters most. While you're awake, you can notice you feel off and take a deep breath. Once you're asleep, nothing is consciously keeping your breathing on track. A person can doze off feeling merely drowsy and then breathe too slowly for hours without waking.

### Why "I've had both before and been fine" isn't reassuring

There's no fixed line you cross. The risk shifts with the hydrocodone dose, how much and how recently you drank, whether you've eaten, your body size and age, whether you have sleep apnea or a lung condition, and whether you've taken anything else that's sedating. A combination that was uneventful one night can go badly on another night when one of those factors changes. That unpredictability is why the official guidance is simply to avoid alcohol rather than to name a "safe" number of drinks.

### How your body breaks hydrocodone down

Your liver clears hydrocodone mainly through two enzymes. One, called **CYP3A4**, turns most of it into an inactive product. Another, called **CYP2D6**, turns a smaller share into **hydromorphone**, a stronger opioid. People vary a lot in how active these enzymes are, and many common medicines can speed them up or slow them down. Some antibiotics, antifungals, and HIV medicines slow CYP3A4, which can raise hydrocodone levels in the blood. The hydrocodone label specifically warns about this.

This matters for alcohol because it means two people on the same prescription can end up with quite different amounts of opioid in their system. Someone with a slower liver, liver disease, or an interacting medicine may already be closer to the edge than they realize before a single drink enters the picture.

### Extended-release hydrocodone

Long-acting forms, **Hysingla ER** and **Zohydro ER**, are built to release hydrocodone slowly over 12 to 24 hours. Each pill holds a much larger dose than an immediate-release tablet. If anything makes that dose release too fast, a person can absorb a large amount at once.

Regulators take this seriously. Labels for extended-release hydrocodone tell patients not to drink alcohol or use medicines that contain alcohol while taking them. More broadly, the FDA asked for an extended-release opioid called Palladone (a form of hydromorphone) to be withdrawn in 2005 after testing showed alcohol could make it release its drug far faster than intended. Modern products are designed and tested with this in mind, but the safe assumption is still the label's: no alcohol with a long-acting opioid.

## What the Research and Official Warnings Say

This isn't a theoretical concern. The guidance from regulators is consistent and clear.

- **A boxed warning.** In 2016 the FDA required its strongest warning on prescription opioids about the risk of combining them with benzodiazepines (drugs like Xanax and Valium) and other central nervous system depressants, a group that includes alcohol. The warning lists profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death as possible results.
- **The patient label is direct.** Hydrocodone medication guides tell patients not to drink alcohol while using the medicine, and not to combine it with other sedating drugs unless their prescriber is managing it.
- **Combination overdoses are common.** Public health data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) have repeatedly shown that many opioid overdose deaths involve more than one substance, and alcohol is one of the substances that often shows up alongside opioids.
- **Controlled studies show the effect.** A study in healthy volunteers published in the journal *Anesthesiology* in 2017 found that adding alcohol to a single dose of oxycodone, a close relative of hydrocodone, reduced breathing more than oxycodone alone, with stronger effects in older participants. There's no reason to expect hydrocodone to behave very differently, since they act on the same receptors.

The US Drug Enforcement Administration moved hydrocodone combination products from Schedule III to the stricter Schedule II in 2014, reflecting how seriously regulators view its risks. That's mainly about misuse rather than alcohol, but it's a good reminder that this is a strong medicine, not a mild one.

## Norco, Vicodin, and Lortab: Two Risks in One Pill

Most hydrocodone prescriptions in the US are combination pills that pair hydrocodone with **acetaminophen**. That includes Norco, Vicodin, Lortab, and many generics labeled "hydrocodone/APAP." Drinking on these brings a second, separate problem on top of the breathing risk.

Acetaminophen is processed by your liver, and a small part of each dose becomes a toxic by-product that the liver has to neutralize. Regular heavy drinking makes the liver produce more of that by-product and lowers its ability to clean it up. That combination is the most common route to drug-related acute liver failure in the US. We explain the chemistry in detail in our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol).

In 2011, the FDA asked makers of prescription combination products to cap acetaminophen at 325 mg per tablet, partly to reduce accidental liver injury. That helped, but it didn't remove the risk, especially because acetaminophen hides in so many other products. If you take a hydrocodone/acetaminophen pill:

- **Don't add Tylenol** or store-brand acetaminophen on top of it.
- **Check cold, flu, and sleep medicines** such as NyQuil, DayQuil, and "PM" products. Many contain acetaminophen, and the night-time ones also contain a sedating antihistamine that adds to the drowsiness.
- **Look for "acetaminophen," "APAP," or "paracetamol"** on every label, and count them all toward your daily total.
- **Ask your pharmacist** what your total daily acetaminophen comes to, especially if you have liver disease or drink regularly.

### Hydrocodone with ibuprofen

Some prescriptions pair hydrocodone with **ibuprofen** instead (the brand Vicoprofen has been one example). These skip the acetaminophen liver issue but bring a different one. Ibuprofen and alcohol both irritate the stomach lining, and together they raise the risk of stomach bleeding. Our [ibuprofen and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) covers that interaction. The breathing risk from the hydrocodone part is unchanged.

### Hydrocodone cough medicine

Hydrocodone also appears in some prescription cough syrups and extended-release cough suspensions. The dose is lower than in pain pills, but it's the same drug acting on the same breathing centers, and these products carry the same warning about alcohol and other sedatives. In 2018, the FDA restricted prescription opioid cough and cold medicines to adults 18 and older because of the risks. If you've been prescribed one, treat it with the same caution as a hydrocodone pain pill.

## How Long After Hydrocodone Can You Drink?

There's no single waiting time that's right for everyone, and you should be wary of any website that gives you an exact number of hours as if it applies to you. What can be said in general:

- **Pain relief and the drug in your body are different things.** Immediate-release hydrocodone usually relieves pain for about 4 to 6 hours, but the drug and its active by-products stay in your body longer than that. Feeling that the pill has "worn off" doesn't mean it's gone.
- **Extended-release forms last much longer.** Hysingla ER is designed as a once-daily pill and Zohydro ER as a twice-daily pill, so the drug is in your system around the clock while you take them.
- **Your own body changes the timeline.** Age, liver and kidney function, body size, and other medications that affect liver enzymes can all slow how fast you clear hydrocodone.
- **The safest plan is not to drink on any day you take it.** If you've finished your prescription, ask your prescriber or pharmacist how long to wait before having alcohol. They can give you an answer based on the exact product and dose.

If you take hydrocodone only as needed, the same rule applies. A dose taken "just for tonight" still interacts with drinks you have that evening.

## Can You Have Just One Drink on Hydrocodone?

The label answer is no, and that's the answer we'll give too. There's no established safe amount of alcohol to combine with hydrocodone. One drink may well cause no obvious harm for some people on some nights, but nobody can tell you in advance whether you're one of them on a given night. The cost of being wrong is not a bad hangover. It's a breathing emergency while you sleep.

If you've already had a drink and then realized you're due for a dose, don't take the hydrocodone on top of it. Call your pharmacist or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) and ask what to do. If you're in pain, they can help you think through options. If anyone is having trouble staying awake or breathing, call 911.

## Who Is at Highest Risk

Anyone can get into trouble with this combination, but the danger is higher if you:

- **Are older.** Older adults tend to clear opioids more slowly and are more sensitive to their effects on breathing.
- **Have sleep apnea, COPD, asthma, or another lung or breathing condition.** Your breathing already has less room to spare.
- **Recently started hydrocodone or had your dose increased.** The first few days on a new dose are when unexpected sedation is most likely.
- **Take an extended-release form.** Each pill holds a larger dose.
- **Have liver or kidney disease.** The drug may build up more than expected.
- **Take other sedating medicines.** That includes benzodiazepines such as [Xanax](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol), [gabapentin](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol), [muscle relaxers](/never-hungover/muscle-relaxers-and-alcohol), sleep medicines, and sedating antihistamines. Each one adds to the load on your breathing.
- **Take another opioid.** Combining opioids, such as hydrocodone with [tramadol](/never-hungover/tramadol-and-alcohol) or [oxycodone](/never-hungover/oxycodone-and-alcohol), stacks the same effect.
- **Have never taken opioids before.** People without any tolerance are more vulnerable to breathing effects.

If any of these describe you, it's especially worth a direct conversation with your prescriber about alcohol before you start or continue hydrocodone.

## Other Dangers of Mixing the Two

Breathing is the biggest risk, but it isn't the only one.

- **Vomiting while sedated.** Both alcohol and opioids can cause nausea. If someone is deeply sedated and vomits, they may not be able to clear their airway.
- **Falls and injuries.** Combined dizziness and poor coordination raise the risk of falls, which is especially serious for older adults.
- **Driving.** Hydrocodone alone can impair driving, particularly when you're new to it. Adding alcohol makes it much worse. Don't drive or operate machinery if you've taken either, let alone both.
- **Liver strain from combination pills.** As covered above, the acetaminophen in Norco, Vicodin, and Lortab adds a liver risk when you drink.
- **Hidden alcohol.** Some liquid medicines, including certain cough and cold syrups and mouthwashes, contain alcohol. Labels for extended-release hydrocodone specifically mention avoiding medicines that contain alcohol. Ask your pharmacist if you're unsure about a product.

## Warning Signs of an Overdose: What to Do Right Now

An opioid-and-alcohol overdose can look like someone just "sleeping it off." Learn to tell the difference.

**Call 911 immediately if someone who has taken hydrocodone and alcohol:**

- Can't be woken up, or wakes only briefly and drifts off again
- Is breathing very slowly, shallowly, or irregularly, or has stopped breathing
- Is making unusual deep snoring, choking, or gurgling sounds
- Has blue, gray, or pale lips or fingertips
- Has pinpoint (very small) pupils
- Has a limp body or cold, clammy skin
- Is very confused or can't speak clearly

**While you wait for help:**

1. **Call 911 first.** Tell the dispatcher the person may have taken an opioid and alcohol.
2. **Give naloxone if you have it.** Follow the instructions on the package. For nasal spray, that means spraying it into one nostril.
3. **Try to keep them awake and breathing.** Say their name loudly and rub their breastbone firmly with your knuckles.
4. **Put them in the recovery position** if they're breathing but not alert: on their side, top knee bent, head tilted slightly back. This helps stop them choking if they vomit.
5. **Stay with them** until help arrives. If they stop breathing and you know how, start rescue breathing or CPR, and follow the dispatcher's instructions.

Most US states have Good Samaritan laws that offer some legal protection to people who call 911 during an overdose. Don't let worry about trouble stop you from calling.

For signs that alcohol alone has reached a dangerous level, see our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs).

### What naloxone can and can't do

**Naloxone** (sold as Narcan and other brands) is a medicine that knocks opioids off their receptors and can restore breathing within minutes. Narcan nasal spray was approved for over-the-counter sale in the US in 2023, so you can buy it at most pharmacies without a prescription. If anyone in your home takes hydrocodone, keeping naloxone on hand is a sensible precaution, and the FDA has encouraged prescribers to discuss it with patients.

But it has limits worth knowing:

- **It doesn't reverse alcohol.** A person who mixed both can still be dangerously sedated after naloxone works on the opioid part.
- **It can wear off before the opioid does.** This is a real risk with extended-release hydrocodone. Someone can wake up after naloxone and then slip back into overdose an hour later.
- **A second dose may be needed.** Package instructions explain when to give another.
- **It's not a reason to skip 911.** The person needs medical care even if they seem to recover.

## Managing Pain Without Mixing

Most people searching "hydrocodone and alcohol" aren't planning anything reckless. Often they have a wedding, a holiday, or a work event coming up during a short prescription after surgery or an injury, and they want to know what's possible. Here's a practical way to think about it:

- **Talk to your prescriber ahead of time.** Tell them about the event. They may adjust your plan, suggest a non-opioid option for that day, or tell you how long you'd need to wait after your last dose. That decision belongs with them, because it depends on your dose, your recovery, and your health.
- **Ask about non-opioid pain relief.** For many kinds of pain, prescribers combine or switch to options like acetaminophen or NSAIDs as recovery progresses. Each has its own alcohol considerations, covered in our [alcohol and medications hub](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications).
- **Choose not to drink at the event.** Skipping alcohol for a few days or weeks while you recover is the simplest way to remove the risk completely.
- **Don't skip doses to "make room" for drinking.** Stopping and restarting pain medicine around alcohol can leave you in uncontrolled pain and lead to taking more later. If you want to change how you take your medicine, ask your prescriber.

If you're taking hydrocodone long term for chronic pain, alcohol is worth discussing at your regular appointments. Your prescriber can look at your full medication list and help you weigh the trade-offs. If you're finding it hard to stay off alcohol while on opioids, say so to your doctor. That's important medical information, and they can help.

## DHM and Other Supplements Are Not Protection

This site covers DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and hangovers. We want to be clear about where it fits here: **it doesn't.**

- **There's no good evidence that DHM makes alcohol safer to combine with hydrocodone.** No supplement has been shown to protect against opioid-and-alcohol respiratory depression.
- **DHM may act on the same calming system.** Early animal research suggests DHM interacts with GABA receptors, the same "slow down" system alcohol and many sedatives affect. It hasn't been studied alongside opioids in people.
- **Don't add it without asking.** If you take hydrocodone, check with your prescriber or pharmacist before adding DHM or any other supplement, including sleep or relaxation products such as kava, valerian, or melatonin combinations.

Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers which medicines need extra caution with supplements more generally.

## The Bottom Line

- Don't drink alcohol while taking hydrocodone. Both slow your breathing, and together the effect can be fatal, most often during sleep.
- The FDA requires a boxed warning about combining opioids with alcohol and other sedating drugs. There's no established safe amount.
- Norco, Vicodin, and Lortab also contain acetaminophen, which adds a liver risk when you drink. Don't add other acetaminophen products on top.
- Extended-release forms like Hysingla ER and Zohydro ER hold larger doses and last 12 to 24 hours, so the risk window is longer.
- Ask your prescriber or pharmacist how long to wait after your last dose before drinking. The answer depends on your product and on you.
- Keep naloxone at home if anyone there takes opioids. If someone can't be woken or is breathing slowly, call 911 and give naloxone if you have it.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking hydrocodone?**

No. Hydrocodone labels tell you not to drink alcohol while taking it, and the FDA requires a boxed warning on opioids because combining them with alcohol or other sedating drugs can cause severe drowsiness, dangerously slow breathing, coma, and death. Both hydrocodone and alcohol slow the part of the brain that controls breathing, and together the effect can be much stronger than either alone. If you've already had a drink, don't take a dose on top of it. Call your pharmacist or Poison Control for advice, and call 911 for slow breathing or trouble staying awake.

**How long after taking hydrocodone can I drink alcohol?**

There's no single waiting time that applies to everyone. Immediate-release hydrocodone pills like Norco and Vicodin relieve pain for roughly 4 to 6 hours but stay in your body longer than that, and extended-release forms such as Hysingla ER and Zohydro ER are designed to last 12 to 24 hours per dose. Your age, liver and kidney function, and other medicines also change how fast you clear it. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist for an answer based on your exact product and dose, and don't drink on any day you take hydrocodone.

**Is it safe to drink on Norco or Vicodin?**

No. Norco, Vicodin, and Lortab contain hydrocodone plus acetaminophen (the drug in Tylenol). Drinking on them carries two risks: dangerously slowed breathing from the hydrocodone and alcohol together, and added strain on your liver from the acetaminophen and alcohol together. Don't take Tylenol, NyQuil, or other acetaminophen products on top of these pills either, because the acetaminophen adds up.

**What happens if you mix hydrocodone and alcohol?**

Effects can range from extra drowsiness, dizziness, slurred speech, and poor coordination to confusion, very slow or shallow breathing, loss of consciousness, and death. The breathing problem is most dangerous during sleep, when the person may not wake up to correct it. Vomiting while heavily sedated is another danger, because the person may not be able to protect their airway. If someone can't be woken or is breathing slowly, call 911 and give naloxone if you have it.

**Does naloxone (Narcan) work on a hydrocodone and alcohol overdose?**

Naloxone can reverse hydrocodone's effect on breathing, so give it if you have it. It does not reverse alcohol, so a person may still be dangerously sedated afterward. Naloxone can also wear off before the hydrocodone does, especially with extended-release products, so the person can slip back into overdose. Always call 911, even if they wake up. Narcan nasal spray has been sold over the counter in the US since 2023.

**Can one beer on hydrocodone hurt you?**

It can. There's no established safe amount of alcohol to combine with hydrocodone, and how much risk one drink carries depends on your dose, the product, your age, whether you have sleep apnea or a lung condition, and whether you take other sedating medicines. That unpredictability is why the label says to avoid alcohol rather than naming a limit. If you're unsure about something you've already had, ask a pharmacist.

**Is hydrocodone cough syrup also dangerous with alcohol?**

Yes. Prescription cough medicines that contain hydrocodone carry the same warning about alcohol and other sedatives as hydrocodone pain pills. The dose is smaller, but the effect on breathing is the same kind of effect, and it adds to alcohol's. Don't drink while you're using one, and don't combine it with other sedating cold or sleep products unless your prescriber or pharmacist has said it's okay.

**Is it safe to take DHM with hydrocodone?**

Don't combine them unless your doctor or pharmacist has approved it. Early animal research suggests DHM acts on GABA receptors, the same calming system that alcohol and many sedatives affect, and it hasn't been studied alongside opioids in people. There's no good evidence that DHM makes alcohol safer to mix with hydrocodone, and it is not protection against an overdose.
